name: The Slippery Slope
aliases: The thin end of the wedge
statement: Claim one small step must lead, unstoppably, to some disastrous end, without showing why.
statementAccent: must lead, unstoppably, to some disastrous end
meaning: The slippery slope is an argument that a relatively small first step or action will inevitably lead, through a chain of related events, to a significant and usually undesirable outcome, without providing sufficient evidence that this chain reaction will actually occur. Picture sliding uncontrollably down a slope once the first step is taken. It becomes a fallacy when the claimed chain of causation is merely asserted rather than justified, with the inevitability of the terrible end assumed instead of argued. Though, not every slippery-slope argument is fallacious: when there is good evidence that one step really will lead to the next, the form can be a legitimate warning. A very common device in politics, law, and ethics debates, it turns on whether each link in the chain is supported.
mechanism: The argument strings together a sequence of steps, claiming that permitting the first makes the next, and then the next, and ultimately a catastrophic final step, inevitable or nearly so. Its whole force depends on the strength of the links: if each transition is well supported by evidence, the argument is sound; if the links are weak or merely asserted, it is fallacious. There are two main varieties. The causal slippery slope claims one event will physically bring about the next in a chain of cause and effect. The conceptual or judgmental slippery slope, related to the sorites paradox, claims that once a distinction is blurred at the edge there is no principled place to stop, so a gradual erosion becomes unstoppable. In both, the fallacy lies in assuming inevitability without justification.

examples.text: Arguing that legalizing one thing will inevitably lead to legalizing worse things and then catastrophe, without showing the steps are actually likely, is a fallacious slippery slope.
When strong evidence shows one step genuinely tends to cause the next, a slippery-slope warning can be a legitimate, non-fallacious argument.
Claiming that blurring a distinction leaves no principled place to stop, a sorites-like erosion, is the conceptual variety of the slippery slope.

variants.name: The causal slippery slope
variants.text: The form asserting a chain of cause and effect, that one event will bring about the next until an undesirable end is reached.

variants.name: The conceptual slippery slope
variants.text: The form, akin to the sorites paradox, holding that once a distinction is relaxed there is no non-arbitrary point at which to halt the erosion.

whyItMatters: The slippery slope is a very common rhetorical device in debates over politics, law, and ethics, invoked whenever a change is opposed on the grounds of where it might lead. Recognising it is a key critical-thinking skill, because it is powerful precisely when it substitutes a vivid, frightening endpoint for an actual argument about likelihoods. Yet it is not always a fallacy, which makes it especially instructive: the task is to examine each link in the chain and ask whether the transitions are genuinely likely or merely asserted. Understanding the slippery slope thus teaches people both to resist scare-mongering by unsupported chains and to take seriously well-evidenced warnings about precedent and gradual erosion.

working.text: test whether each step in the claimed chain is actually likely to lead to the next, rather than accepting the endpoint's inevitability on assertion.
distinguish a chain of cause and effect from a sorites-like erosion of a distinction, since each demands different scrutiny.
accept a slippery-slope argument when strong evidence backs the chain, since a well-supported version is a legitimate warning, not a fallacy.

limits: The slippery slope is fallacious only when the causal or conceptual chain is asserted without adequate support, so a well-evidenced version, where one step genuinely tends to lead to the next, is a legitimate argument rather than a fallacy. Judging which case applies requires weighing the actual probabilities of each transition, which can be uncertain and contested. The metaphor of sliding down a slope is ancient, traceable to Cicero, and the argument has no single modern originator, so it is a long-recognised pattern rather than a coinage. As an informal fallacy, its diagnosis depends on the substantive strength of the links, not on the form alone.
misreadings: Not every slippery-slope argument is a fallacy; whether it is depends on whether the chain of steps is supported by evidence, so a well-justified version is a legitimate warning. The fallacy lies specifically in asserting inevitability without argument, not in raising the possibility of consequences. And the argument comes in causal and conceptual forms, so treating it purely as a chain of physical causes misses the sorites-like version about the erosion of distinctions, which fails or succeeds by different standards.
origin: A classic informal fallacy whose metaphor of an unstoppable descent is ancient, appearing in Cicero, with no single modern originator; its validity turns on whether the causal or conceptual chain is supported by evidence.
